newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan asks for delay on U.S. bank/commerce mix.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan asks for delay on U.S. bank/commerce mix.

text.p: Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan on Saturday warned against moving too quickly on mixing banking and commerce, recommending a staggered approach to one of the most controversial issues in the debate over U.S. bank law reform.

Banks should be allowed to enter other financial businesses such as insurance and securities underwriting before being allowed unlimited entry into non-financial, commercial businesses, Greenspan said in prepared remarks for a speech to the Independent Bankers Association of America.

"New legislation should not attempt to accomplish too much too soon," he said. "The Board believes it is prudent to delay, or to implement in stages, broad authorization of nonfinancial activities for banking companies."
"We want to be sure of the smooth functioning of integrated financial activity before we address potential combinations of banking and commerce," he added.

How much to limit banks' commercial activities is one of the last unresolved questions hanging over the financial modernization debate. Many groups, including the independent bankers and House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, strongly oppose any mixing of financial and nonfinancial companies.
Aside from discussing financial modernization, Greenspan also issued a modest warning about a relaxation of bank underwriting standards.

Other regulators, notably Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig, have expressed such concerns in the past, especially regarding the syndicated loan market. Non-bank entrants in that market have driven down loan rates and led to more relaxed underwriting standards, regulators have said.
Greenspan echoed those observations but described the problem as modest.

"Recent evidence of thin margins and increased non-bank competition in portions of the syndicated loan market, as well as other indicators, suggest some modest underwriting laxity has a tendency to emerge during good times," Greenspan said, alluding to the economy's strong performance over the past several years.
"This suggests the need for a mild caution that bankers maintain sound underwriting standards and pricing practices in their lending activities," he added.

Greenspan also discussed his view of the Fed's role in regulating financial holding companies under various financial modernization proposals. Under some proposals, the Fed would be the primary regulator of financial service companies engaged in banking and other other services. But other bills would leave the Fed out.
The Fed would not excessively intrude on diversified companies if it was designated the primary regulator, Greenspan argued.

"We believe there has been some considerable misunderstanding of our basic philosophy of holding company suprvision," Greenspan said. "The focus of the Fed's inspections of non-bank activities of bank holding companies is to gain a sense of the overall strength of the individual units and their interrelations with each other and the bank."

"Only if there is a major deficiency in (the adequacy of risk management and internal controls) would we intend for a bank holding company inspection to become in any signficant way 'intrusive,' and the number of such intrusive inspections of non-banking activities should be quite small if managements are following prudent business practices," Greenspan said.
